newsitem.title: USA: USDA FY98 budget may crimp food aid, local offices.
newsitem.headline: USDA FY98 budget may crimp food aid, local offices.

text.p: The fiscal 1998 budget for the U.S. Agriculture Department is likely to call for cuts in the major U.S. food aid program and in the number of local offices in farm country, analysts and congressional staff workers said.
The White House was slated to release its proposals at 0800 EST/1300 GMT Thursday.
Analysts said "Freedom to Farm" payments appeared safe from attack. Farmers would get $5.8 billion in fiscal 1998.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has hinted the budget may give farmers longer periods to repay crop loans.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle, of South Dakota, has proposed allowing a five-month extension of the loans and removing the ceiling on loan rates but gotten little support.

Congressional staff workers have said a cut of $100 million was likely in the "Food for Peace" program, which was allotted $1.1 billion for this fiscal year. The cut would come in Title I, the long-term concessional sales program.

More local offices of the Farm Service Agency, which runs the farm subsidy program, would be closed, according to analysts and congressional staffers. The closings would be in addition to an ongoing plan to streamline operations.
At present, USDA intends to reduce its workforce, now 104,500 people, to about 101,000 in 1999.
A new round of user fees, totaling $300-$400 million, would be proposed for meat inspection, one analyst said.
Glickman has said he expects a "lean but austere" budget that "protects our priorities" but has not provided details.
The $90 million a year Market Access Program has drawn fire as "corporate welfare." Deputy Secretary Richard Rominger said Monday that funding for the program would be defended.
Congress limited the Export Enhancement Program, the major U.S. export subsidy program, to $100 million this year.

Under the 1996 farm policy law, EEP was authorized for $500 million in fiscal 1998. Analysts said budget cutters might eye EEP for savings since there have been no cut-price grain sales since mid-1995.
"The real issue of the year is the CRP (Conservation Reserve Program)," said one analyst.

Congress might take a hand, either by curtailing funding or rewriting legislation, if unhappy with new operating rules for the reserve. Conservation groups say the rules, to be released soon, make too much land eligible, thereby squandering money and failing to protect fragile land.
